title: Matrix multiplication exponent
formal: Determine the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega =\inf \{\tau \in \mathbb{R} : \exists C>0 \forall n\ge 2, s(n)\le C n^{\tau}\}\), where \(s(n)\) is the minimum number of arithmetic gates computing every entry of the product of two arbitrary \(n\times n\) complex matrices exactly, in the circuit model below.
definitions: The inputs are \(2n^{2}\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\). The required \(n^{2}\) output polynomials are \(c_{ij}=\sum _{k=1}^{n} a_{ik} b_{kj}\). A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with binary addition, subtraction, and multiplication gates; any complex constants and unrestricted reuse of intermediate values are allowed. Size counts arithmetic gates, including operations involving constants. Input nodes, constant nodes, and output designations are not gates. No division, order comparisons, branching, approximation, or randomization is permitted. A different circuit may be chosen for every n: this is the standard nonuniform arithmetic-complexity formulation over C. The cost of encoding a complex number in bits is outside this model. The elementary lower bound \(s(n)\ge n^{2}\) for \(n\ge 2\) follows because the \(n^{2}\) distinct non-input output polynomials require distinct gates. The infimum defines a real number between 2 and 3. It need not be attained: determining \(\omega\) does not require an \(O(n^{\omega})\) circuit bound. An exact candidate w must have upper bounds \(s(n)=O_{\varepsilon}(n^{w+\varepsilon})\) for every \(\varepsilon >0\) and no bound \(s(n)=O(n^{\tau})\) for any \(\tau <w\).
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- \omega |\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.
why: This exponent measures the asymptotic arithmetic cost of a fundamental operation and governs many other algebraic and graph algorithms. Determining its value would locate the limit of savings from shared computation.

importance.reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.

progress.text: Strassen gives \(O(n^{\log _{2}7})\) arithmetic operations, establishing that cubic multiplication is not optimal.

Alman proves that the universal method applied to any Coppersmith–Winograd tensor cannot yield an exponent below 2.16805. This is a limitation of that tensor-based route, not a proof that omega exceeds two.
The SODA paper More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication gives omega<2.371339 by extending the combination-loss analysis. The original preprint appeared in April 2024.

Dupont and coauthors report omega<2.371177. Section 4 describes rounding the optimized parameters to rationals and verifying directed bounds for logarithms; it says the verification repository is being prepared. This catalogue has not independently replayed that certificate.
Version 3 of More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication incorporates the new optimization bound. The remaining gap to two persists.

status_note: The latest primary upper bound located through 10 September 2026 is the reported omega<2.371177 from August 2026. It leaves the omega=2 question open. The model is exact arithmetic over C; the catalogue has not independently reproduced the numerical certificate. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The usual algorithm computes \(n^{2}\) inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The scientific target is the value of the exponent, whether it equals two or is larger. The familiar \(\omega =2\) conjecture specifies one possible answer. Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, an upper bound may approach it with a different circuit family and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Exact scalar arithmetic over a fixed field separates this quantity from approximate numerical multiplication and hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

There are also lower bounds on what specific tensor methods can achieve. For example, Alman’s universal-method barrier for Coppersmith–Winograd tensors prevents that route from reaching exponent two. It is not a lower bound on all arithmetic circuits for matrix multiplication. The distinction leaves room for different starting tensors or mathematical constructions.

sentences: Matrix multiplication asks for every entry of the product of two arbitrary square matrices over the complex numbers.
The target is the infimum arithmetic-circuit exponent \(\omega\).
The well-known conjecture \(\omega =2\) is one possible value, rather than the only answer considered by this card.
The infimum can be approached without an algorithm attaining its endpoint exponent.
The Lean benchmark accepts a certified value with absolute error at most 0.01, while the saved literature supplies upper bounds and barriers for specific methods.
